paras: Every section of a scientific paper has a reader in mind, and the methods section has the strangest one of all. The introduction is written for somebody deciding whether to care. The discussion is written for somebody who wants to argue. The methods section is written for a person you will never meet, working in another building, who has to run your experiment again next year without asking you a single question. Everything odd about the way it is written comes from that one fact.

That is why the people disappear. Nobody writes I put the tubes in the incubator, because the reader does not need to know that it was you, and next year it will not be. The tubes were incubated. The samples were collected in March. The control group was not treated at any point. The thing that had something done to it moves to the front of the sentence, the person is removed, and what is left is the only part that can be repeated. It is not modesty and it is not bad style. It is the section doing its job.

The second thing that carries the whole section is order, and order is not obvious from the verbs alone. Two steps written side by side can be simultaneous, or one can depend on the other having already finished, and the reader cannot tell which unless you say so. That is the work done by prior to, following, once and subsequently, and by the form that marks something as already finished before the step you are describing: the apparatus had been calibrated before the first measurement was taken. Take those words out and the section is still true, and no longer reproducible.

Which is where most first drafts fail, and it is worth knowing before you write your own. The steps are usually all there, and the problem is that they are only listed. Somebody who was in the room can read the draft and follow it perfectly, because they already know what happened, so the writer never notices. The reader in another building cannot. If you take one habit from this section, take this one: write it, then read it as somebody who was not there.

items: The methods section is written for a reader who was not in the room.
It is written for a person you will never meet, in another building, who has to run the experiment again without asking you anything.
The person is removed from the sentence because naming yourself is impolite.
It is not modesty and it is not bad style. The person is removed because next year the person will be somebody else, and only what was done can be repeated.
The order of the steps can be worked out from the verbs alone.
Two steps written side by side can be simultaneous, or one can depend on the other having finished. The reader cannot tell which unless the sequence words say so.
A draft can be completely true and still not be reproducible.
The steps are usually all there and only listed. Take the sequence words out and the section is still true, and no longer reproducible.
A writer normally notices this problem while reading their own draft.

listenings.text: Before anybody presents anything, I want to say something about the paper we tried to repeat last month, because I think it is the most useful thing that happened to this group all year. We chose it because the result was interesting and because it looked simple. Four weeks later we had spent about nine hundred reais of consumables and we still did not have their result, and here is the part that matters: we are now fairly sure the work is fine. The paper is not. Three things were missing. The temperature at which the samples were stored between collection and analysis, which turned out to be the whole thing. Whether the replicates were pooled before or after the first measurement, which the text simply does not say. And a single sentence about the control group that could be read two ways. Nobody was hiding anything. Somebody wrote the section, read it back, and it made perfect sense to them, because they had been standing there. So when you write yours, the test is not whether it is true. The test is whether somebody in another building could run it on a Tuesday without emailing you.

Hi, it is me, I am leaving this now because you asked me to keep an eye on your samples while you were away and I want you to have the order right rather than my summary of it. So. On Monday the tubes were taken out of the freezer and thawed on the bench, not in the water bath, because the water bath was broken again. They were left for about forty minutes. Prior to any of that, and this is the bit you did not ask for, the whole rack had already been relabeled, because two of your labels had come off in the freezer and I did not want to guess. On Tuesday the replicates were pooled, three into one, and then the first measurements were taken. Following that, everything went back at minus twenty. Your control group was not touched at any point, which I assume is what you wanted. One thing I am not sure about, and you should write it down before you forget: I do not know whether the tubes had been thawed once before, in June. Ask the person who ran it then, because I genuinely do not know, and it belongs in your methods.
